paragraphs.text: Form No. HCJD/C-121 ORDER SHEET LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT W.P.No.927 of 2026. Areej Sohail Bhutta. Versus Federation of Pakistan, etc. S.No.of order / Proceeding Date of Order/ Proceeding Order with signature of Judge, and that of parties counsel, where necessary 03.11.2026. Mr. Asad Sami Butt, Advocate for the petitioner. Mr. Shahzada Irfan Awan, Assistant Attorney General. Mr. Muhammad Nasir Chohan, Addl. Advocate General. The petitioner, who is a practicing Advocate by profession, has invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court in the capacity of a public-spirited citizen, claiming that, during the course of her professional practice, she came across certain female clients who allegedly narrated their ordeals of non-consensual sexual conduct within their matrimonial relationships. According to the petitioner, such experiences brought to her attention amount to an alleged deficiency in the existing legal framework governing the offence of rape, particularly with regard to the absence of a distinct statutory treatment of sexual violence within marriage. On the basis of such professional encounters and her understanding of the constitutional guarantees of dignity, equality and security of person, she has approached this Court seeking directions to the Federal and Provincial Governments to undertake appropriate legislative measures, including amendments to Sections 375 and 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, so as to provide a specific legal framework addressing what she describes as the deficient legal regime concerning marital rape. She further asserts that the existing legal position requires reconsideration in the light of fundamental rights, principles of natural justice and the Injunctions of Islam.

The controversy raised through the instant petition requires examination of the constitutional distribution of powers amongst the three organs of the State, namely, the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary. It is an established constitutional principle that the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 is the supreme law of the land and all organs of the State are required to function within the limits of authority assigned to them thereunder. The Legislature is entrusted with the responsibility of making laws, the Executive with their implementation, whereas the Judiciary interprets the law and ensures that the actions of the other organs remain within constitutional bounds. Although judicial review is an essential feature of constitutional governance, the same does not authorize a Court to assume the legislative functions assigned to the elected representatives of the people.

Before proceeding further, it is necessary to observe here that Article 199 of the Constitution empowers the High Court to issue appropriate directions for the enforcement of fundamental rights guaranteed under Chapter I of Part II of the Constitution. The jurisdiction, though wide in its scope, is nevertheless subject to constitutional limitations. A direction for enforcement of an existing constitutional or statutory obligation stands on an entirely different footing from a direction requiring the Legislature to enact a particular law, prescribe a new offence or introduce a specific legislative policy. The former falls within the recognized domain of judicial review, whereas the latter ordinarily falls within the exclusive legislative domain. In Miss Benazir Bhutto v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 1988 SC 416), the august Supreme Court recognized the significance of public interest litigation and observed that the traditional rules of locus standi may be relaxed where enforcement of fundamental rights of a group or class of persons is involved. Nevertheless, the exercise of constitutional jurisdiction remains subject to the requirements prescribed by the Constitution. Public importance, by itself, does not confer upon a Court the authority to undertake functions constitutionally entrusted to another organ of the State.

The petitioner has invoked various considerations relating to the dignity, security and protection of women within matrimonial relationships. In this regard, Articles 9, 14 and 25 of the Constitution deserve consideration. Article 9 guarantees security of person; Article 14 protects the dignity of man and, subject to law, the privacy of home; whereas Article 25 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of law and prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex. Furthermore, Article 25(3) expressly authorizes the State to make special provisions for the protection of women and children. Article 34 also requires steps to ensure the full participation of women in all spheres of national life. These constitutional guarantees cannot be disregarded while examining matters concerning the protection of women.

At the same time, Article 35 of the Constitution requires the State to protect marriage, the family, the mother and the child. The constitutional protection of the institution of marriage, however, cannot be interpreted as conferring an unrestricted license to inflict violence upon any spouse. Equally, the protection of individual dignity and personal security must be examined within the constitutional and legal framework governing matrimonial relationships. Both considerations require a harmonious interpretation rather than an approach which unnecessarily places one constitutional value in conflict with another. So far as the existing criminal law is concerned, Section 375 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, as substituted through the Criminal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 (Act LVI of 2021), defines the offence of rape and identifies the circumstances in which the relevant acts constitute such offence, including acts committed against the will or without the consent of the affected person. The provision also defines consent as an unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated through words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication. Section 376 provides punishment for the offence. Significantly, the substituted text of Section 375 does not expressly reproduce a general exemption for a husband merely on account of the subsistence of a valid marriage. However, the precise application and interpretation of these provisions in a particular matrimonial situation would depend upon the statutory ingredients and facts of the individual case.

In addition, the legal framework is not confined to the Pakistan Penal Code alone. Various enactments have been introduced for the protection of women against domestic and other forms of violence. For instance, the Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act, 2016, provides protective remedies against domestic, sexual, psychological and economic abuse, while corresponding protective legislation has also been enacted in other provinces, including Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. These enactments demonstrate that the protection of women within domestic and matrimonial relationships is already a subject of legislative attention. The existence, scope and adequacy of these enactments, however, must be assessed according to their respective provisions and territorial application.

The petitioner's reliance upon certain foreign legislative models also requires a careful constitutional examination. Merely because a particular legislative arrangement has been adopted in another country does not make it automatically applicable to Pakistan. Nor can a foreign legislative model be introduced into the domestic legal system without examining its compatibility with the Constitution, the existing statutory framework, the social and legal structure of the country and the Injunctions of Islam. Foreign legislation or judicial precedents may, where appropriate, provide comparative assistance, but they cannot override the Constitution or substitute the legislative judgment of the competent Pakistani Legislature.

In this context, the Islamic character of the constitutional framework assumes particular significance. Article 2A incorporates the Objectives Resolution as a substantive part of the Constitution. Article 227(1) mandates that all existing laws shall be brought into conformity with the Injunctions of Islam as laid down in the Holy Quran and Sunnah and that no law shall be enacted which is repugnant to such Injunctions. However, Article 227(2) further provides that effect shall be given to the provisions of Article 227(1) only in the manner provided in Part IX of the Constitution. Thus, the constitutional mechanism for examining the Islamic conformity of proposed legislation cannot be bypassed or replaced by an individual judicial assumption.

Another important aspect of the matter concerns the legislative competence of Parliament and the Provincial Assemblies. Article 142(b) of the Constitution expressly confers upon both Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) and the Provincial Assemblies the power to make laws with respect to criminal law, criminal procedure and evidence. Consequently, the subject raised by the petitioner falls within a legislative field in which the Constitution recognizes the competence of the respective legislatures. It is for the competent legislative forum to examine the necessity, scope, ingredients, safeguards and consequences of any proposed amendment, keeping in view the constitutional scheme and the requirements of justice. The Executive may initiate or facilitate legislative proposals, but the enactment of primary legislation remains the function of the competent Legislature.

The question whether an additional offence, a separate statutory provision or a further protective mechanism is required is essentially a matter of legislative policy. Such policy considerations involve multiple aspects, including the definition of the proposed offence, the requisite ingredients, evidentiary requirements, procedural safeguards, protection of complainants, prevention of misuse and the harmonious relationship between criminal law and matrimonial rights and obligations. These matters require comprehensive deliberation by the competent legislative forums. A constitutional Court cannot substitute its own legislative judgment for that of Parliament or a Provincial Assembly.

In Tika Iqbal Muhammad Khan and others v. General Pervez Musharraf Chief of Army Staff, Rawalpindi and others (PLJ 2008 SC 500), the august Supreme Court recognized the principle that a Court cannot issue a mandamus compelling the Legislature to enact a particular law. Similarly, the doctrine of separation of powers, as recognized in Jurists Foundation through Chairman v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Ministry of Defence and others (PLD 2020 Supreme Court 1), requires judicial restraint in matters falling within the constitutionally assigned domain of the elected branches of the State, while preserving the power of judicial review where constitutional limits are transgressed.

In the present case, the petitioner has not challenged any particular statutory provision as being violative of fundamental rights, nor has any specific unlawful action or failure to perform an existing statutory obligation by a competent authority been demonstrated which may warrant issuance of a constitutional direction under Article 199 of the Constitution. The principal relief sought is, in substance, a direction to the Federal Government and Provincial Governments to undertake a particular legislative exercise and introduce a legislative model of the petitioner's choice. Such a direction would amount to judicial interference in the legislative process and would be inconsistent with the constitutional distribution of powers.

It is, however, clarified that decision of the instant petition shall not be construed as an endorsement of any form of violence, coercion or abuse within matrimonial relationships, nor shall it be interpreted as a declaration that the dignity, bodily integrity and constitutional rights of a woman stand diminished by reason of marriage. Equally, this judgment shall not preclude Parliament or any Provincial Assembly from examining the matter and undertaking appropriate legislative measures, if considered necessary, in accordance with the Constitution and the Injunctions of Islam. The Court has confined itself to the limited question whether the particular legislative direction sought by the petitioner can be issued in exercise of constitutional jurisdiction.

For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds that no case is made out for issuance of a direction compelling the Federal Government or the Provincial Governments to enact legislation in the manner proposed by the petitioner. The relief sought falls within the domain of the competent Legislature and cannot be granted through the exercise of constitutional jurisdiction. Consequently, the instant petition, being devoid of merit to the extent of the relief claimed, is dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs. (ABHER GUL KHAN) Judge Approved for reporting JUDGE *Abdul Rehman *
